Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

Section II Reading Comprehension

Part A

Text 1

It is tempting to assume that the accumulation of plastic in the ocean is simply a
consequence of careless disposal, and that the appropriate response is therefore to
strengthen the rules governing waste. That account is not wrong, but it is incomplete, and
the incompleteness matters. A substantial proportion of the plastic now circulating in ocean
currents never passed through a household bin. It entered the water as industrial pellets,
as fibres shed from synthetic clothing during washing, or as fragments of fishing gear lost
or abandoned at sea. Each of these pathways implies a different remedy. Pellet loss is best
addressed at the point of production, fibre shedding at the design stage of textiles, and
abandoned gear through changes in the economics of fishing rather than through appeals to
conscience. The tendency to treat marine plastic as a single problem has therefore obscured
the fact that it is a cluster of problems with distinct causes. Researchers have documented
the consequences with increasing precision. Fragments are now found in sediments, in Arctic
ice, and in the tissue of animals that never encounter a human settlement. Whether these
fragments cause harm is a separate and genuinely disputed question. Some studies report
effects on feeding and reproduction; others find none. What is not disputed is that the
quantity continues to rise, and that the measures adopted so far have not altered the trend.
The implication is uncomfortable. A problem defined too broadly may be addressed only by
measures too general to work.
